title: Theories of Reaction Rates
description: Complex mechanisms, unimolecular reactions, collision theory, transition state theory and kinetic isotope effects.
overview: Chemical kinetics at the general chemistry level describes how fast reactions go and uses the Arrhenius equation to fit the temperature dependence. Physical chemistry asks why: what determines the pre-exponential factor and the activation energy, and how can we calculate a rate constant from the properties of molecules, as we calculate an equilibrium constant from partition functions?

This chapter answers with three levels of theory. It first solves the kinetics of more complex mechanisms (consecutive, parallel and opposing steps), then explains unimolecular reactions (Lindemann–Hinshelwood), and finally derives rate constants from collision theory and from transition state theory, with kinetic isotope effects as the experimental test.
objectives: Solve the kinetics of consecutive, parallel and opposing reactions.
Explain the pressure dependence of unimolecular rate constants (Lindemann–Hinshelwood).
Calculate collision frequencies and rate constants from collision theory, and the diffusion-controlled limit.
Use the Eyring equation to find activation parameters ΔH‡, ΔS‡ and ΔG‡.
Predict kinetic isotope effects from zero-point energies.

sections.title: Consecutive, parallel and opposing reactions
body: Real mechanisms combine elementary steps, and the integrated rate laws can be solved exactly for the simplest combinations. Three patterns recur.
For A → B → C with first-order constants k₁ and k₂ and starting with only A, the concentrations are [A] = [A]₀e^{−k₁t}, and

The intermediate B rises, passes through a maximum and decays. If k₂ ≫ k₁, B never accumulates and its concentration is small and almost constant: the steady-state approximation. The product C forms at a rate set by the slower step, the rate-determining step.

example.title: Intermediate maximum
example.problem: For A → B → C with k₁ = 0.10 s⁻¹ and k₂ = 0.020 s⁻¹, find the time at which [B] is a maximum and the maximum fraction.
example.solution: t_max = ln(0.10/0.020)/(0.10 − 0.020) = ln 5/0.080 = 20 s. [B]_max/[A]₀ = 5^{−0.020/0.080} = 5^{−0.25} = 0.67. Two thirds of the material is present as B at the maximum.

body: If A forms two products in competing first-order steps, A → B (k₁) and A → C (k₂), A decays with k_obs = k₁ + k₂, and the product ratio [B]/[C] = k₁/k₂ is fixed for all times. The **branching ratio** gives the selectivity, and the temperature dependence of the ratio is controlled by the difference of the activation energies: raising T favors the product with the higher activation energy.

For a reversible first-order reaction A ⇌ B, with k_f and k_r, the approach to equilibrium follows a single exponential: [A] − [A]_eq = ([A]₀ − [A]_eq) e^{−(k_f + k_r)t}. The **relaxation time** τ = 1/(k_f + k_r) is shorter than either individual lifetime. At equilibrium the rates match, so K = k_f/k_r, which links kinetics to thermodynamics. The sum, not the difference, of the rate constants determines the speed of relaxation, which is the basis of temperature-jump experiments on fast equilibria.

example.title: Relaxation to equilibrium
example.problem: For A ⇌ B with k_f = 0.50 s⁻¹ and k_r = 0.10 s⁻¹, find K and the relaxation time, and the equilibrium composition starting from pure A.
example.solution: K = 0.50/0.10 = 5. τ = 1/(0.60 s⁻¹) = 1.7 s. At equilibrium [B]/[A] = 5, so the mixture is 83% B.

check.q: In parallel first-order reactions A → B and A → C, the ratio [B]/[C] is…
For A ⇌ B, the relaxation to equilibrium has rate constant…

sections.title: Unimolecular reactions: Lindemann–Hinshelwood and RRKM
body: Experiments show that many gas-phase reactions of a single molecule, such as the isomerization of cyclopropane or the decomposition of N₂O₅, are first order at high pressure. How does a molecule get enough energy to react, if no other molecule takes part in the rate law? Lindemann (1922) proposed that the energy comes from collisions with another molecule M, and the reaction happens in a separate step:

eq: A + M ⇌ A* + M     (k₁, k₋₁)   collisional activation and deactivation
A* → P     (k₂)   reaction of the energized molecule

body: Applying the steady-state approximation to A*:

list: **High pressure** (k₋₁[M] ≫ k₂): the activation equilibrium is maintained, and the rate = (k₁k₂/k₋₁)[A], first order, with k_∞ = k₁k₂/k₋₁.
**Low pressure** (k₋₁[M] ≪ k₂): every A* reacts before it can be deactivated, so the rate = k₁[A][M], second order overall: the collision is rate-limiting.

body: As the pressure falls, the observed first-order constant falls from k_∞: the **falloff region**. A plot of 1/k_uni against 1/[M] is a straight line (1/k_uni = k₋₁/(k₁k₂) + 1/(k₁[M])) in the Lindemann scheme. Experiments show the falloff begins at a much higher pressure than predicted, and the plot curves. The reason is that the model treats all energized molecules as reacting with the same rate constant k₂, whereas in fact k₂ depends strongly on how much energy the molecule has, and on how many ways (vibrational modes) the energy can be distributed.

**RRKM theory** (Rice–Ramsperger–Kassel–Marcus) corrects this: it assumes that the energy of A* is rapidly randomized among all its vibrations (intramolecular vibrational redistribution), and the rate constant k(E) is the probability that enough energy flows into the reaction coordinate, proportional to the ratio of the number of states of the transition state to the density of states of the molecule. Larger molecules, with more modes, hold the energy longer, and so the falloff region shifts to lower pressure: a small molecule such as CH₃NC → CH₃CN is in the falloff region at 10 torr, but a large one is already at high pressure at 10⁻³ torr. RRKM theory predicts the full pressure- and temperature-dependence and is the standard model for atmospheric and combustion reactions.

example.title: Pressure dependence
example.problem: A unimolecular gas reaction has k_∞ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and falls to half that value at 0.50 atm. What is k_uni at 0.10 atm in the Lindemann model?
example.solution: k_uni = k_∞ [M]/([M] + k₂/k₋₁). Half of k_∞ at 0.50 atm means k₂/k₋₁ = 0.50 atm (in pressure units). At 0.10 atm: k_uni = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.10/(0.10 + 0.50) = 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.

check.q: At low pressure, the Lindemann–Hinshelwood rate law is…
Why does RRKM theory give a better description than the Lindemann model?
check.a: k₂ depends on the energy of A* and the number of vibrational modes among which it is shared
wrong: It uses a different activation energy
It treats the reaction as bimolecular

sections.title: Collision theory of rate constants
body: Simple collision theory gives the rate constant of a bimolecular gas reaction A + B → P as the rate at which A and B collide with enough energy. Two molecules collide if their centers come within the **collision cross-section** σ = πd², where d is the mean of the molecular diameters. The number of collisions per unit volume and time between A and B is Z_AB = σ c̄_rel [A][B] with the mean relative speed c̄_rel = √(8kT/πμ). The fraction of the collisions that have kinetic energy along the line of centers above a threshold E_a is e^{−E_a/RT}, so

The factor P, the **steric factor**, is the fraction of collisions in which the orientation allows reaction. P = 1 would mean that every sufficiently energetic collision reacts. The pre-exponential factor of the Arrhenius equation is then A = P σ c̄_rel N_A, and it should rise as √T.

example.title: Collision-theory prefactor
example.problem: For molecules with σ = 0.40 nm² and μ = 20 amu, find the maximum A (P = 1) at 298 K.

eq: A = σ c̄_rel N_A = (4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²)(562 m s⁻¹)(6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) = 1.35 × 10⁸ m³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 1.4 × 10¹¹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹

solution: Measured pre-exponential factors are often smaller: P is about 0.16 for 2NOCl → 2NO + Cl₂ and about 10⁻⁶ for reactions of large molecules that must collide in a specific way. A reaction with a P larger than 1 shows that the theory underestimates the cross-section, as in the ‘harpoon’ mechanism for K + Br₂ (long-range electron jump), where P ≈ 4.

body: In solution, a molecule undergoes many collisions with solvent before meeting a reactant. If every encounter leads to reaction, the rate is limited by how quickly A and B diffuse together, the **diffusion-controlled limit**: k_d = 8RT/(3η) (the Smoluchowski result for equal-size molecules in a solvent of viscosity η). For water at 298 K (η = 8.9 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s) it gives k_d = 8 × 8.314 × 298/(3 × 8.9 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.4 × 10⁶ m³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 7.4 × 10⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹, close to the observed rate constants for acid–base reactions of H₃O⁺ with OH⁻ (1.4 × 10¹¹, which is faster since protons hop by the Grotthuss mechanism), and for diffusion-controlled reactions such as fluorescence quenching, radical recombination and the binding of ligands by enzymes at the speed limit (carbonic anhydrase, kcat/K_M ≈ 10⁸ M⁻¹ s⁻¹). Slower reactions are activation-controlled.

check.q: What does the steric factor P represent in collision theory?
check.a: The fraction of energetic collisions that have the proper orientation

check.q: What limits the rate constant of a diffusion-controlled reaction in water?
check.a: The rate at which the reactants diffuse together

sections.title: Transition state theory and the Eyring equation
body: **Transition state theory (TST)**, developed by Eyring, Evans and Polanyi (1935), calculates the rate constant from the properties of the reactants and of the **activated complex** at the top of the barrier on the potential energy surface. It makes two assumptions: the activated complex is in quasi-equilibrium with the reactants, and the complex falls apart through its one unbound motion (the reaction coordinate, a vibration with an imaginary frequency) at a rate of kT/h per complex. The result, the **Eyring equation**:

Here κ (about 1) is the transmission coefficient. The universal factor kT/h (6.2 × 10¹² s⁻¹ at 298 K) is the rate at which any activated complex passes through the barrier. The reaction is then described by thermodynamic parameters of activation: the **enthalpy of activation** Δ‡H (the energy barrier), the **entropy of activation** Δ‡S (how much more or less ordered the complex is than the reactants) and the Gibbs energy Δ‡G = Δ‡H − TΔ‡S. A bimolecular association has a strongly negative Δ‡S (two molecules combine into one complex: −80 to −150 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), and a unimolecular dissociation that loosens the structure has Δ‡S > 0.

From the Eyring equation, a plot of ln(k/T) against 1/T (an **Eyring plot**) is a straight line of slope −Δ‡H/R and intercept ln(k_B/h) + Δ‡S/R. The relation to the Arrhenius activation energy is E_a = Δ‡H + RT for a solution reaction (and Δ‡H + 2RT for a gas-phase bimolecular reaction).

example.title: Activation free energy
example.problem: A first-order reaction has k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 298 K. Find Δ‡G. With k = 8.0 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ at 328 K, find Δ‡H and Δ‡S.

eq: kT/h = 6.21 × 10¹² s⁻¹ at 298 K;   Δ‡G = −RT ln(kh/kT) = −2.478 kJ × ln(3.22 × 10⁻¹⁶) = 88.4 kJ mol⁻¹

solution: Then Δ‡S = (Δ‡H − Δ‡G)/T = (97.2 − 88.4)/298 = +30 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The positive entropy of activation suggests a loosening transition state, consistent with a dissociative step.

body: TST gives the right form and useful quantitative accuracy when the potential energy surface is known, and a very successful framework for interpreting measured Δ‡H and Δ‡S. Its weaknesses: some trajectories recross the barrier (κ < 1), tunneling is ignored (important for H transfer), and it is classical for the motion along the reaction coordinate. Variational TST and trajectory calculations on computed surfaces address these.

check.q: What is the slope of an Eyring plot (ln(k/T) against 1/T)?

check.a: A more ordered transition state, as in a bimolecular association

sections.title: Kinetic isotope effects
body: Replacing an atom with a heavier isotope leaves the electronic potential energy surface unchanged but lowers the vibrational frequencies and so the zero-point energies. The change in rate is the **kinetic isotope effect**, KIE = k_light/k_heavy, and it is a powerful probe of which bonds change in the rate-determining step.

list: A **primary KIE** arises when the bond to the isotope is broken or formed in the rate-determining step. In the transition state the C–H stretch becomes the reaction coordinate and loses its zero-point energy, while the C–D bond starts lower in energy, so the barrier for C–D cleavage is higher by (at most) the difference in zero-point energies.

A **secondary KIE** arises when the isotope is on an atom whose bonding changes but is not broken (an sp³ → sp² change in hybridization gives k_H/k_D about 1.1–1.25 and sp² → sp³ gives about 0.8–0.95). It tells the hybridization change at the reacting carbon.
**Solvent isotope effects** (H₂O versus D₂O) test whether proton transfer is involved.

example.title: Maximum C–H/C–D effect
example.problem: The C–H stretch is 2900 cm⁻¹ and the C–D stretch 2100 cm⁻¹. Estimate the maximum k_H/k_D at 298 K, assuming the stretching zero-point energy is entirely lost at the transition state.
example.solution: ΔZPE = ½(2900 − 2100) cm⁻¹ = 400 cm⁻¹ = 400 × 0.01196 = 4.78 kJ mol⁻¹. k_H/k_D = exp(4780/(8.314 × 298)) = e^{1.93} = 6.9. Observed primary effects range from 1 to about 7 at 25 °C; values above about 10 point to hydrogen **tunneling**, as in the enzyme soybean lipoxygenase, where k_H/k_D ≈ 80. KIEs fall with rising temperature, as ΔZPE/RT shrinks.

body: Heavy-atom effects are small but measurable (¹²C/¹³C about 1.04, ³²S/³⁴S about 1.02) and give the extent of bond breaking in the transition state. The measurement of a KIE shows whether a C–H bond cleaves in the rate-determining step of an oxidation by a cytochrome P450 enzyme, or whether an elimination follows E2 or E1 mechanisms.

check.q: What causes the primary kinetic isotope effect?
check.a: The C–D bond has a lower zero-point energy, so it requires more energy to reach the transition state
wrong: D is heavier and therefore slower to collide
The electronic surface changes with isotope

check.q: A k_H/k_D of 50 at room temperature most strongly suggests…

quiz.q: In A → B → C, k₁ = 0.20 s⁻¹ and k₂ = 0.050 s⁻¹, starting with pure A. At what time does [B] reach its maximum?
quiz.why: t_max = ln(k₁/k₂)/(k₁ − k₂) = ln 4/0.15 = 9.2 s. Dividing by k₁ alone gives 6.9 s, and dividing by the sum k₁ + k₂ gives 5.5 s.

quiz.q: A decays by two parallel first-order paths, A → B with k₁ = 6.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and A → C with k₂ = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the half-life of A?
quiz.why: A decays with k₁ + k₂ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, so t½ = ln 2/(8.0 × 10⁻³) = 87 s. Using only k₁ gives 116 s and only k₂ gives 347 s.

quiz.q: A forms B by a path with E_a = 80 kJ mol⁻¹ and C by a path with E_a = 60 kJ mol⁻¹, both first order. How does the ratio [B]/[C] change if the temperature is raised?
quiz.a: It increases, since the path with the higher activation energy speeds up more
wrong: It decreases, since the lower-barrier path dominates at high T
It is unchanged, since [B]/[C] = k₁/k₂ is fixed for all times
quiz.why: The ratio is constant in time, but it equals k₁/k₂ = (A₁/A₂)exp(−(E₁ − E₂)/RT), which rises with T when E₁ > E₂. Being fixed during one run does not make it independent of temperature.

quiz.q: For A ⇌ B, the equilibrium constant is K = 4.0 and k_r = 0.050 s⁻¹. What is the relaxation time toward equilibrium?
quiz.why: k_f = K k_r = 0.20 s⁻¹, so τ = 1/(k_f + k_r) = 1/0.25 = 4.0 s. Using k_f alone gives 5.0 s, k_r alone 20 s, and the difference of the constants 6.7 s.

quiz.q: A unimolecular reaction has k_∞ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, and k_uni falls to half of this at 0.20 atm. In the Lindemann model, what is k_uni at 1.0 atm?
quiz.why: k_uni = k_∞[M]/([M] + k₂/k₋₁) with k₂/k₋₁ = 0.20 atm, so k_uni = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.0/1.2 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹. The 3.3 × 10⁻⁵ comes from inverting the fraction.

quiz.q: In the Lindemann scheme, a plot of 1/k_uni against 1/[M] is a straight line. What is its intercept?
quiz.why: 1/k_uni = k₋₁/(k₁k₂) + 1/(k₁[M]). As 1/[M] → 0 (high pressure), k_uni → k_∞, so the intercept is 1/k_∞. The slope is 1/k₁.

quiz.q: Which assumption is central to RRKM theory?
quiz.a: Energy in an energized molecule is rapidly shared among all its vibrations
wrong: The energy stays in the bond that will break
Every energized molecule reacts with the same rate constant
Only the translational energy of the collision partner is transferred
quiz.why: Fast intramolecular vibrational redistribution makes k(E) depend on the energy and on how many modes share it. A single constant k₂ for all energized molecules is the Lindemann assumption RRKM replaces.

quiz.q: Two molecules have mean relative speed √(8kT/πμ). What is this speed at 298 K for a reduced mass of 5.0 amu?
quiz.why: √(8 × 4.116 × 10⁻²¹/(π × 8.30 × 10⁻²⁷)) = 1.12 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The speed scales as μ^{−1/2}, so a reduced mass of 20 amu would give half of this, 5.6 × 10² m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: A reaction has σ = 0.50 nm², mean relative speed 1.1 × 10³ m s⁻¹ and steric factor P = 0.010. What is the collision-theory A in M⁻¹ s⁻¹?
quiz.why: A = Pσc̄N_A = 0.010 × 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.1 × 10³ × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.4 × 10⁶ m³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ = 3.4 × 10⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. Without P the value is 3.4 × 10¹¹, and 3.4 × 10⁶ forgets the conversion from m³ to liters.

quiz.q: According to simple collision theory, how does the pre-exponential factor change when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 1200 K?
wrong: It increases by a factor of 16
quiz.why: A = Pσ√(8kT/πμ)N_A varies as √T, and √4 = 2. The exponential factor e^{−E_a/RT} carries the main temperature dependence, not A.

quiz.q: How does the diffusion-controlled rate constant 8RT/3η at 298 K change if the solvent viscosity is ten times that of water?
quiz.a: It falls by a factor of 10 to about 7 × 10⁸ M⁻¹ s⁻¹
wrong: It rises by a factor of 10
It does not change, since T is fixed
quiz.why: k_d is inversely proportional to η, so ten times the viscosity gives one tenth of the rate constant, about 7 × 10⁸ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. The rate constant is not limited by temperature here, since T is the same.

quiz.q: A first-order reaction has k = 1.0 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ at 298 K (kT/h = 6.2 × 10¹² s⁻¹). What is Δ‡G?
quiz.why: Δ‡G = −RT ln(kh/kT) = 2.478 kJ × ln(6.2 × 10¹⁴) = 2.478 × 34.0 = 84 kJ mol⁻¹. The value 11 kJ comes from −RT ln k alone, which leaves out the universal factor kT/h.

quiz.q: A solution reaction has an Arrhenius activation energy of 75.0 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. What is Δ‡H?
quiz.why: For a reaction in solution E_a = Δ‡H + RT, so Δ‡H = 75.0 − 2.5 = 72.5 kJ mol⁻¹. Subtracting 2RT would be correct only for a gas-phase bimolecular reaction.

quiz.q: An Eyring plot of ln(k/T) against 1/T (k/T in s⁻¹ K⁻¹) has intercept 22.0. Given ln(k_B/h) = 23.76, what is Δ‡S?
quiz.why: The intercept equals ln(k_B/h) + Δ‡S/R, so Δ‡S = R(22.0 − 23.76) = −14.6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Taking R × 22.0 forgets the ln(k_B/h) term.

quiz.q: Which statement about transition state theory is correct?
quiz.a: It treats the motion over the barrier classically, so tunneling is not included
wrong: It assumes the activated complex is stable with real frequencies in every mode
It gives a rate that depends on the reactant but not on the temperature through kT/h
It requires the transmission coefficient κ to be exactly 1 in all cases
quiz.why: TST ignores tunneling, which matters for hydrogen transfer, and recrossing of the barrier makes κ less than 1. The complex has one imaginary frequency, the reaction coordinate.

quiz.q: The C–H and C–D stretching wavenumbers of a bond are 3100 and 2250 cm⁻¹. If the zero-point energy of this stretch is entirely lost in the transition state, what is the maximum k_H/k_D at 298 K?
quiz.why: ΔZPE = ½(3100 − 2250) = 425 cm⁻¹ = 5.08 kJ mol⁻¹, and k_H/k_D = exp(5080/(8.314 × 298)) = 7.8. Omitting the ½ gives 60, and losing only half the ZPE difference in the transition state gives 2.8.

quiz.q: A solvolysis shows k_H/k_D = 1.18 when deuterium is on the carbon that becomes a carbocation, with no C–H bond broken. What does it suggest?
quiz.a: The carbon changes hybridization from sp³ to sp² in the rate-determining step
wrong: The C–H bond is broken in the rate-determining step
The carbon changes from sp² to sp³ in the rate-determining step
The reaction proceeds by hydrogen tunneling
quiz.why: A secondary effect of 1.1–1.25 is typical of sp³ → sp² (a looser out-of-plane bend in the transition state). Values below 1 indicate sp² → sp³, and tunneling would give far larger effects.

quiz.q: A primary k_H/k_D is 6.0 at 298 K and arises only from zero-point energy. What is it expected to be at 350 K?
quiz.why: ln(k_H/k_D) = ΔZPE/RT, so it scales as 1/T: 1.79 × 298/350 = 1.53 and the ratio is e^{1.53} = 4.6. The ratio falls as T rises; scaling it linearly gives 5.1, and using T in the numerator gives 8.2.

summary: A → B → C: B reaches a maximum at t_max = ln(k₁/k₂)/(k₁ − k₂). Parallel reactions have a fixed product ratio k₁/k₂. Opposing reactions relax with k_f + k_r and K = k_f/k_r.
Lindemann–Hinshelwood: first order at high pressure (k_∞ = k₁k₂/k₋₁), second order at low pressure, and a falloff in between. RRKM theory includes the energy dependence of k₂.
Collision theory: k = Pσ√(8kT/πμ)N_A e^{−E_a/RT}. In solution the diffusion limit is k_d = 8RT/3η, about 7 × 10⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ in water.
Eyring: k = κ(kT/h)exp(Δ‡S/R)exp(−Δ‡H/RT). The Eyring plot gives Δ‡H and Δ‡S, and E_a = Δ‡H + RT in solution.
KIEs: C–H/C–D up to about 7 at 25 °C from zero-point energy differences. Larger values signal tunneling.

problems.q: For A → B → C, k₁ = 0.050 min⁻¹ and k₂ = 0.50 min⁻¹. Show that the steady-state approximation applies and estimate [B]/[A] at long times.
problems.solution: Since k₂ ≫ k₁, B decays much faster than it forms. After the first few minutes [B] ≈ (k₁/k₂)[A] = 0.10[A] (the steady-state value), so B is never more than about 10% of A.

problems.q: An enzyme-catalyzed reaction between a substrate and an enzyme with encounter radius 0.5 nm has a measured k of 5 × 10⁷ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. Is the reaction diffusion-controlled? (η = 8.9 × 10⁻⁴ Pa s, 298 K.)
problems.solution: k_d = 8RT/3η = 7.4 × 10⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. The measured value is 100 times smaller than this limit, so the reaction is not diffusion-controlled: the reaction step itself (activation) is slower than the encounter.
problems.a: No: k is about 150 times below the diffusion limit.

problems.q: The rate constant of an SN2 reaction in solution is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 300 K and 2.4 × 10⁻³ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 330 K. Find Δ‡H and Δ‡S.
problems.a: Δ‡H = 84.5 kJ/mol; Δ‡S ≈ −40 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (negative, as expected for a bimolecular reaction).

problems.q: The C–H and C–D stretching frequencies for a reacting bond are 3000 and 2200 cm⁻¹. Estimate the maximum KIE at 298 K and at 400 K.
